title: Pathophysiology: Neurologic Function—Cerebral Perfusion, Stroke, Seizures and Deterioration
html:
The nervous system depends on continuous oxygen and glucose delivery, intact electrical signaling, controlled intracranial volume, and coordinated networks. Neurologic deterioration may result from vascular interruption, bleeding, edema, infection, inflammation, toxins, metabolic disturbance, seizure, trauma, or degeneration. The RN compares the client with baseline, recognizes time-sensitive patterns, stabilizes airway and circulation, and communicates precise changes rather than relying on a single score or diagnosis label.

Learning goals

  • Relate cerebral blood flow, autoregulation, intracranial pressure, and cerebral perfusion pressure.
  • Explain cerebral edema, declining intracranial compliance, and herniation risk.
  • Compare ischemic stroke, transient ischemia, intracerebral hemorrhage, and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
  • Connect vascular territory and brain function to focal deficits.
  • Explain seizure initiation, postictal findings, and status epilepticus.
  • Distinguish focal structural findings from diffuse metabolic or toxic dysfunction.
  • Describe demyelination, neurodegeneration, and neuromuscular transmission failure.
  • Prioritize sudden deficit, declining consciousness, seizure, meningismus, and respiratory failure.

Neurons require uninterrupted delivery and stable chemistry

Brain tissue has high metabolic demand and limited energy storage. Reduced oxygen, glucose, or blood flow quickly impairs ATP-dependent ion pumps. Sodium and water enter cells, membrane potentials fail, excitatory neurotransmitters accumulate, calcium-dependent enzymes activate, and oxidative and inflammatory injury spread. Early dysfunction may be reversible; sustained severe injury produces cell death.

Systemic hypoxemia, anemia, hypoglycemia, hypotension, fever, seizure, electrolyte disturbance, hepatic or renal failure, toxins, and medications can cause diffuse cerebral dysfunction. A focal lesion more often produces asymmetric motor, sensory, language, visual, or coordination findings, although presentations can overlap.

Cerebral perfusion depends on pressure and resistance

Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) = mean arterial pressure (MAP) − intracranial pressure (ICP). CPP is the pressure gradient that supports cerebral blood flow, but actual flow also depends on vascular resistance, blood viscosity, oxygen content, carbon dioxide, and local metabolic demand.

Cerebral autoregulation adjusts arteriolar tone to maintain relatively stable flow across a range of systemic pressures. Chronic hypertension can shift the autoregulatory range, while trauma, ischemia, severe hypercapnia, and other injury may impair autoregulation. Both hypotension and indiscriminate rapid blood-pressure reduction can reduce cerebral perfusion in susceptible clients; excessive pressure may worsen edema or bleeding. Follow condition-specific targets and protocols.

Carbon dioxide is a potent cerebral vasodilator. Hypercapnia can increase cerebral blood volume and ICP; marked hypocapnia causes vasoconstriction and can reduce cerebral flow. Ventilation changes therefore affect both acid–base physiology and intracranial hemodynamics.

The skull contains a fixed total volume

The adult skull contains brain tissue, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid. When one component increases, cerebrospinal fluid displacement and venous blood outflow can initially compensate. Once this reserve is exhausted, small additional volume increases can cause a steep rise in ICP.

Causes include hematoma, tumor, cerebral edema, hydrocephalus, impaired venous drainage, infection, and diffuse traumatic injury. Rising ICP lowers CPP, which can worsen ischemia and edema, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Tissue shifts across rigid intracranial boundaries can compress the brainstem and cause herniation.

Edema mechanisms differ

Cytotoxic edema reflects cellular swelling after energy failure, as in early ischemia or severe metabolic injury. Vasogenic edema follows blood–brain barrier disruption, allowing fluid and proteins into extracellular space, as around tumors, inflammation, trauma, or later ischemic injury. Interstitial edema can accompany hydrocephalus as cerebrospinal fluid moves across ventricular surfaces.

Because treatment varies by mechanism, do not assume every form of cerebral edema responds to the same intervention. Monitor the trajectory and the client's airway, ventilation, circulation, sodium, osmolality, temperature, glucose, and neurologic examination.

A change in consciousness is often an early warning
New restlessness, confusion, slowed responses, or increasing somnolence can precede dramatic pupil, motor, or vital-sign changes. Confirm sedation and metabolic factors, but treat an unexplained decline as urgent neurologic deterioration.

Recognize rising ICP and possible herniation

Possible findings include worsening headache, vomiting, altered level of consciousness, new focal deficit, unequal or poorly reactive pupils, abnormal posturing, seizure, and changes in respiratory pattern. The classic combination of widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular respirations is a late finding and should never be awaited.

Immediate priorities are airway and oxygenation, hemodynamic support, neutral head and neck alignment when not contraindicated, minimizing avoidable stimulation or venous obstruction, rapid escalation, and preparation for diagnostic and prescribed ICP-directed treatment. Avoid hip or neck flexion, tight devices, fever, severe coughing or straining, and uncoordinated care that can increase intrathoracic or intracranial pressure.

Ischemic stroke creates a core and a threatened penumbra

Arterial thrombosis or embolism reduces blood flow to a brain territory. Tissue with critically low flow becomes the infarct core; surrounding tissue with partial collateral flow may remain dysfunctional yet salvageable for a limited time. Progressive clot effects, poor collaterals, hypotension, hypoxemia, fever, hyperglycemia, and edema can expand injury.

Sudden unilateral weakness or numbness, facial asymmetry, speech or language difficulty, visual loss, gaze deviation, severe imbalance, or neglect suggests acute stroke. Posterior circulation stroke may present with diplopia, dysphagia, vertigo, ataxia, altered consciousness, or crossed findings and can be missed by a face-arm-speech screen.

Determine the exact time symptoms began or the last known well time, activate the stroke pathway, check glucose promptly, protect the airway, keep the client safe from oral intake until swallowing is assessed, and prepare for urgent brain and vascular imaging. Symptom improvement does not make the event safe to observe routinely.

TIA is a warning event, not a benign diagnosis

A transient ischemic attack produces temporary focal neurologic dysfunction from ischemia without established infarction on current tissue-based definitions. Symptoms may resolve before evaluation, but early stroke risk can be substantial and urgent assessment is required. Document the exact deficits, timing, duration, vascular risk factors, rhythm history, medications, and return to baseline.

Hemorrhage injures by blood, pressure, and secondary inflammation

Intracerebral hemorrhage directly disrupts tissue, expands mass effect, increases ICP, and triggers inflammatory and toxic effects from blood products. Hematoma expansion can cause rapid deterioration. Hypertension, anticoagulation, vascular malformations, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and other disorders may contribute.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage places blood in the subarachnoid space, often producing abrupt severe headache, vomiting, photophobia, meningismus, loss of consciousness, or focal findings. Complications include rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizures, sodium disturbance, and delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm and other mechanisms.

Ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke cannot be reliably distinguished from symptoms alone. Urgent imaging is essential because treatments differ and some ischemic therapies can be dangerous in hemorrhage.

Brain regions produce recognizable—but imperfect—patterns

  • Dominant hemisphere: aphasia, impaired reading, writing, or calculation, and contralateral weakness or sensory loss.
  • Nondominant hemisphere: neglect, visuospatial impairment, impulsivity, and contralateral deficits.
  • Frontal networks: motor function, initiation, judgment, behavior, and expressive language.
  • Parietal networks: sensory integration, spatial awareness, and skilled actions.
  • Temporal networks: memory, emotion, auditory processing, and receptive language.
  • Occipital cortex: visual fields and visual processing.
  • Cerebellum: coordination, balance, and motor timing.
  • Brainstem: consciousness pathways, cranial nerves, long motor and sensory tracts, breathing, and cardiovascular control.

Localization supports rapid communication but does not replace standardized examination or imaging. Baseline handedness, language, vision, hearing, cognition, and prior deficits matter.

Seizures reflect abnormal synchronized network activity

A seizure results from excessive, hypersynchronous neuronal activity. It may begin focally in one network or involve bilateral networks from onset. Manifestations include motor activity, sensory or autonomic symptoms, behavioral arrest, altered awareness, or subtle eye or facial movements—not only generalized convulsions.

Provoked seizures may occur with hypoglycemia, sodium disturbance, fever, hypoxia, toxin or alcohol withdrawal, infection, acute stroke, trauma, or medication changes. Epilepsy refers to an enduring predisposition to recurrent unprovoked seizures, not every isolated provoked event.

During a seizure, protect the client from injury, support the airway and oxygenation, position safely when possible, note the start time and clinical sequence, and do not restrain limbs or place objects in the mouth. Afterward, reassess breathing, circulation, glucose, neurologic status, injury, and return toward baseline.

Status epilepticus is a time-sensitive emergency

Prolonged or recurrent seizures without meaningful recovery can produce hypoxemia, hyperthermia, acidosis, aspiration, rhabdomyolysis, dysrhythmia, and neuronal injury. Convulsive activity may become subtle while electrical seizure continues. Persistent unexplained altered consciousness after apparent seizure cessation can represent nonconvulsive status and requires urgent evaluation.

Activate emergency protocols, support airway and circulation, obtain glucose, establish monitoring and access, administer prescribed time-sensitive antiseizure therapy, and investigate reversible causes. Monitor respiratory depression, hypotension, rhythm, temperature, and recurrent activity.

Altered mental status requires a broad differential

Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, usually caused by an underlying medical, neurologic, medication, or environmental problem. Dementia is a chronic acquired decline in cognition that interferes with function and is not explained by delirium alone. They can coexist.

New confusion may result from hypoxia, hypoglycemia, stroke, seizure, infection, medication toxicity, withdrawal, pain, urinary retention, constipation, sleep disruption, or renal, hepatic, endocrine, and electrolyte disorders. Do not attribute it automatically to age, dementia, or behavior.

Demyelination slows or blocks signal conduction

Myelin permits rapid saltatory conduction along axons. Central demyelination, as in multiple sclerosis, can produce episodes separated in time and neurologic location, including vision, sensory, motor, coordination, bladder, or cognitive symptoms. Peripheral demyelination can produce ascending weakness, sensory change, and areflexia. Respiratory muscle and autonomic involvement can become life-threatening.

Serial strength, cranial nerve, swallowing, respiratory effort, vital-capacity measures when ordered, and autonomic monitoring are important when weakness is progressing. Oxygen saturation may remain normal until ventilatory failure is advanced.

Neurodegeneration reflects selective network loss

Neurodegenerative disorders accumulate abnormal proteins, synaptic dysfunction, inflammation, and progressive neuron loss in characteristic networks. Parkinsonian disorders prominently affect movement circuits; Alzheimer disease first often disrupts memory networks; motor neuron diseases impair voluntary motor function while sensation may be relatively preserved.

Acute deterioration is not automatically disease progression. Screen for infection, injury, medication effects, dehydration, pain, metabolic disturbance, aspiration, and other reversible stressors. Functional safety, swallowing, mobility, communication, caregiver support, and goals of care are central.

Neuromuscular failure can threaten breathing without lung disease

Damage to motor neurons, peripheral nerves, neuromuscular junctions, or muscle can reduce ventilation, cough, and airway protection. Bulbar weakness increases aspiration risk. Clients may develop shallow breathing, weak voice, difficulty counting or holding the head up, paradoxical abdominal movement, or declining inspiratory force before SpO₂ falls.

Escalate progressive weakness, dysphagia, pooling secretions, ineffective cough, or reduced ventilation promptly. Avoid exhausting the client with repeated testing and prepare for prescribed ventilatory support.

Prioritize the neurologic trajectory
Sudden focal deficit, first or prolonged seizure, rapidly declining consciousness, new unequal pupils, severe abrupt headache, fever with meningismus, progressive weakness with breathing difficulty, or neurologic change during anticoagulation requires immediate escalation.

Translate neurologic physiology into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Establish last known well and baseline, then assess airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, consciousness, pupils, gaze, speech, face, strength, sensation, coordination, headache, seizure activity, medications, trauma, infection, and metabolic data.
  2. Analyze cues: Organize findings as focal or diffuse, acute or chronic, ischemic, hemorrhagic, pressure-related, electrical, inflammatory, toxic-metabolic, degenerative, or neuromuscular.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway failure, acute stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, herniation, status epilepticus, central nervous system infection, severe hypoglycemia, and progressive neuromuscular respiratory failure outrank stable deficits.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan emergency activation, airway and perfusion support, glucose correction, seizure safety, positioning, urgent imaging and laboratories, medication reversal or therapy as prescribed, and serial standardized examinations.
  5. Take action: Stay with the unstable client, record exact timing and changes, protect airway and injury risk, implement the appropriate pathway, and communicate the neurologic trajectory.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess consciousness, pupils, speech, motor and sensory findings, breathing, hemodynamics, glucose, seizure recurrence, swallowing safety, ICP or imaging trends when available, and treatment complications.

Clinical example

A client suddenly develops aphasia and right arm weakness. Glucose is normal and symptoms began 25 minutes ago. The RN documents last known well, activates the stroke pathway, supports airway and circulation, keeps the client from oral intake pending swallowing assessment, obtains a focused standardized examination, and prepares for urgent imaging. When the weakness partially improves, the RN continues the emergency evaluation because transient improvement can represent TIA or fluctuating ischemia rather than resolution of risk.
